Two-to-One Against

A Double-Barrier Binary-Option Analysis of Futures Proprietary-Trading Evaluations

Abstract

Retail traders are sold a futures proprietary-trading-firm ("prop firm") evaluation as a funding opportunity: pay a monthly fee, hit a profit target on a simulated account without breaking a loss rule, and trade the firm's capital for a high profit split. We argue this is the wrong accounting frame. The correct frame is that the firm is writing an exotic derivative and selling it to an unsophisticated counterparty.

We prove that a standard futures evaluation is mathematically identical to a discrete double-barrier one-touch (digital) option written on the trader's cumulative profit-and-loss. Because the contract is denominated in dollars and a futures trader trades a roughly fixed number of contracts, the natural model is arithmetic Brownian motion on P&L, not geometric motion on equity. We take the exact contract from a live $100,000 pricing card — profit target $6,000, max-loss "One Rule" $3,000, $2,000 daily loss limit, 50% consistency, 30-day cycle — whose numbers coincide with the widely advertised $100K futures Combine archetype.

The single most important number falls straight out of the geometry. The target is twice as far as ruin (a 2:1 barrier reward-to-risk). By the gambler's-ruin theorem, a genuinely edgeless trader's probability of ever hitting the target before busting — with no time limit at all — is

\[ P_{\text{pass}}^{\infty}\big|_{\text{zero edge}} = \frac{|D|}{U+|D|} = \frac{3000}{9000} = \frac{1}{3}. \]

The 30-day clock and the rules only subtract from this ceiling. We derive the finite-horizon pass probability in closed form (a Dirichlet heat-kernel spectral expansion), validate it against a 200,000-path Monte-Carlo, and compute the Greeks. Theta is brutal: at realistic risk the pass probability decays from \~0.12–0.16 over the month to effectively zero in the final two days. Vega is positive but capped: an edgeless trader can raise the pass probability by taking more volatility, yet can never beat the 1/3 ceiling — and a skilled trader has a modest interior-optimal volatility that already sits inside the permitted band. Delta and Gamma describe the forced position-sizing dynamics near each barrier.

We then value the whole journey honestly — the funded account is itself a second (trailing) barrier option with capped payouts. Unlike a trader-favourable equity-percentage contract, the 2:1 futures geometry makes the evaluation negative expected value for any trader without a genuine, positive edge: the break-even win rate at 1:1 reward-to-risk is ≈ 50% before costs and clearly above it once fees and slippage are included. The "Responsible Trading" rule set — trailing drawdown, daily loss limit, consistency — functions as a precise cap on volatility \(\sigma\) that acts as an edge filter: the relative pass-probability haircut it imposes falls monotonically with edge, from −93% (negative edge) and −80% (zero edge) to just −16% for a strongly skilled trader, who barely needs variance. It strips the edgeless majority — who could only have passed via variance — while sparing genuine skill. With variance removed, Theta finishes the job. The "responsible" low-volatility scalper the rules nominally reward has, in our simulation, a 1.9% pass rate.

All results are reproducible from the accompanying Python (code/); every quoted number is emitted to data/results.json. We keep the analysis general to futures evaluations; the supplied card is used only as a concrete, canonical instance.

1. Introduction

1.1 The two ways to read a futures evaluation

A modern futures prop firm sells a product that looks like this:

Pay $129/month for a $100,000 "buying-power" simulated account. Grow its P&L to +$6,000 (the profit target) and you are funded, trading our capital for a high split. But if your P&L ever falls to −$3,000 below your high-water mark (the trailing max-loss limit — "Don't Break the One Rule") — or you lose $2,000 in a single day — you fail. To get funded you must also satisfy a 50% consistency rule (no single day may be more than half your total profit). The cycle resets monthly.

The retail reading is "a cheap, fair route to capital; I just have to trade well for a month." The institutional reading is "someone has written me a path-dependent digital option, set the target twice as far as the knock-out, and attached a list of rules that cap how fast I can move." This paper formalises the second reading and shows it is not a metaphor but an identity — and that, for the futures 2:1 structure specifically, the mathematics is decisively against the edgeless buyer.

1.2 Thesis

**A futures prop-firm evaluation is a discrete double-barrier one-touch binary option on cumulative P&L. Its 2:1 barrier geometry caps an edgeless trader's lifetime pass probability at 1/3; the 30-day clock (Theta) and the trailing / daily / consistency rules (a cap on volatility \(\sigma\)) cut it to roughly one in ten; and the funded payoff is itself a capped second barrier option. The result is a structurally negative-expected-value purchase for anyone without a genuine statistical edge — and the rules are precisely the mechanism that filters such traders out.**

1.3 Contributions

  1. A formal dictionary (Section 2) translating every line of the pricing card

into exotic-option notation.

  1. The geometry result (Section 3.3): the 2:1 reward-to-risk fixes the

edgeless ceiling at 1/3 before skill or time is considered.

  1. Closed-form pass probabilities (Section 3): a scale-function result for

the perpetual contract and a Dirichlet heat-kernel spectral expansion for the 30-day contract, validated to Monte-Carlo accuracy.

  1. The Greeks of an evaluation (Section 4): Theta, the capped Vega, Delta,

and Gamma of the pass-probability functional.

  1. A 100,000-path Monte-Carlo study (Sections 5–6) mapping trading style

(win rate, reward-to-risk, dollar risk, skew) to pass probability under the full rule set, with jump-diffusion robustness.

  1. An honest economic valuation (Section 7): the funded account as a capped

second barrier option, the break-even edge, and the volatility filter that is the real house edge.

1.4 A note on intellectual honesty (and what changed from the equity model)

An earlier version of this analysis modelled the underlying as an equity-percentage process with a +8% / −10% target/loss (a 0.8:1 geometry). That structure is mildly trader-favourable in the perpetual limit (eventual pass ≈ 0.58), and we reported — against our own initial hypothesis — that priced as a stand-alone instrument it was roughly fair. The futures card is a different instrument. Its 2:1 dollar geometry inverts the asymmetry: the perpetual edgeless ceiling is 1/3, not 0.58. We re-derived everything in P&L space and report the consequences, which are far more adverse to the buyer and make the predatory reading robust rather than borderline. We flag the model switch explicitly so the two analyses are not confused.

2. The Contract and Its Exotic-Option Identity

2.1 The dictionary

Let the trader's cumulative account P&L at time \(t\) be \(X_t\) (dollars above the starting balance), monitored in trading days \(t \in [0,T]\).

Pricing-card lineSymbolCard valueOption-theoretic object
$100K buying power\(S_0\)$100,000 notionalCollateral / notional (P&L starts at 0)
Profit target\(U\)+$6,000Upper knock-in barrier; one touch triggers the payoff
Max loss (One Rule)\(D\)−$3,000Lower knock-out barrier (trailing high-water-mark)
Barrier reward:risk\(U/|D|\)2 : 1Target is twice as far as ruin
Time limit / cycle\(T\)30 daysMaturity
"Funded"—binaryFixed (digital) payoff \(\Pi\) on knock-in
Daily loss limit\(d\)$2,000 (0.66×)Path constraint that caps \(\sigma\)
Consistency target\(c\)50%Best day ≤ 50% of profit — a further \(\sigma\) cap
Max contract limit—10 mini / 100 microHard cap on per-trade dollar risk \(k\) (hence \(\sigma\))
Profit split\(s\)~90% (capped payouts)Scaling of the funded-phase payoff
Monthly fee / reset\(F\)$129Option premium (recurring)

2.2 The payoff, formally

Define the first-passage times of the P&L process

\[ \tau_U = \inf\{t \ge 0 : X_t \ge U\}, \qquad \tau_D = \inf\{t \ge 0 : X_t \le D_t\}, \]

where \(D_t = \max(\text{peak}_t - 3000,\, 0)\) is the trailing max-loss floor (it ratchets up with the high-water mark and, in the typical implementation, locks at break-even). The trader passes iff

\[ \text{PASS} = \{\tau_U \le T \;\wedge\; \tau_U < \tau_D\} \;\cap\; \{\text{consistency satisfied}\}, \]

and the cash payoff is digital, $\text{Payoff} = \Pi\cdot\mathbf 1_{\text{PASS}} - F\(, with \)\Pi$ the value of being funded (Section 7). The firm is short this digital and long the recurring fee.

2.3 Taxonomy

The instrument is a double-barrier one-touch binary: an American digital / one-touch at \(U\) (you pass the instant P&L tags +$6,000), a down-and-out knock-out at the trailing \(D_t\) (one touch and the contract is dead), and European expiry at \(T\). Barriers are monitored discretely (trade-by-trade), hence discrete double barrier. The consistency rule is a path functional layered on top. For "unlimited-time" account types set \(T=\infty\); the trailing drawdown and daily limit then become the binding constraints (Section 3.3).

3. The Mathematical Framework

3.1 P&L as arithmetic Brownian motion

A futures trader trades a roughly fixed number of contracts, so each trade adds an approximately fixed dollar increment to cumulative P&L. The natural state variable is therefore \(X_t\) itself, modelled as arithmetic Brownian motion with drift,

\[ dX_t = \mu\,dt + \sigma\,dW_t, \qquad X_0 = 0, \]

where \(\mu\) is the dollar drift per day (skill, net of fees) and \(\sigma\) is the dollar volatility per day (risk / position size). This differs deliberately from a geometric-Brownian equity model: there is no volatility drag term, so a genuinely break-even trader has \(\mu = 0\) exactly, and the barriers are fixed dollar levels rather than percentages.

The barriers are \(U = +6000\) and (static reference) \(D = -3000\), a strip of width \(L = U - D = 9000\), with the trader starting a distance \(b = 6000\) below the target and \(a = 3000\) above ruin. The defining asymmetry is \(b = 2a\): the target is twice as far as the knock-out. Everything follows from this.

3.2 Pass probability as a first-passage problem

\[ P_{\text{pass}}(\mu,\sigma,T) = \Pr\big(\tau_U \le T \,\wedge\, \tau_U < \tau_D \mid X_0 = 0\big). \]

We give the perpetual answer first, then the finite-\(T\) spectral series.

3.3 Perpetual contract: the geometry decides

For \(T=\infty\) the scale function of arithmetic BM is \(s(x)=e^{-\theta x}\) with \(\theta = 2\mu/\sigma^2\), and optional stopping gives

\[ \boxed{\;P_{\text{pass}}^{\infty} = \frac{1 - e^{-\theta D}}{e^{-\theta U} - e^{-\theta D}}\;} \qquad\xrightarrow[\mu\to 0]{}\qquad \frac{0-D}{U-D} = \frac{|D|}{U+|D|}. \]

For the edgeless trader (\(\mu = 0\)):

\[ P_{\text{pass}}^{\infty}\big|_{\text{zero edge}} = \frac{3000}{9000} = \frac{1}{3}. \]

Figure 1. Pass probability versus the barrier reward-to-risk \(U/|D|\). Blue: the perpetual (no-time-limit) edgeless probability \(1/(1+U/|D|)\). Red: with the 30-day clock at moderate risk. The 2:1 card sits where a coin-flip trader tops out at 1/3 with no clock — and ~0.12 with one. The old +8%/−10% equity model (0.8:1) sat in trader-favourable territory.

This is the headline the marketing hides: before skill, time, or any rule, the 2:1 geometry caps an honest coin-flipper at one in three. A 1.5:1 account (common on smaller sizes) caps at \(1/2.5 = 0.40\); the old 0.8:1 equity contract sat at 0.56. Geometry alone moves the goalposts by tens of percentage points.

3.4 Finite horizon: the Dirichlet heat-kernel spectral expansion

Adding the clock, we solve the Fokker–Planck equation on the strip \((D,U)\) with absorbing (Dirichlet) boundaries and integrate the probability flux through the upper boundary over \([0,T]\). Shifting to \(y = x - D \in (0,L)\) with start \(y_0 = -D = a\), removing drift with the Doob \(h\)-transform \(p = e^{\frac{\mu}{\sigma^2}(y-y_0) - \frac{\mu^2}{2\sigma^2}t}q\), and expanding the resulting heat equation in \(\sin(n\pi y/L)\) eigenfunctions yields the finite-horizon pass probability

\[ \boxed{\; P_{\text{pass}}(\mu,\sigma,T) = \frac{\sigma^2 \pi}{L^2}\, e^{\frac{\mu}{\sigma^2}(L - y_0)} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (-1)^{n+1}\, n\, \sin\!\frac{n\pi y_0}{L}\, \frac{1 - e^{-\beta_n T}}{\beta_n} \;},\qquad \beta_n = \frac{\mu^2}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\Big(\frac{n\pi}{L}\Big)^2 . \]

The lower-boundary flux gives the bust probability \(P_{\text{bust}}\); the residual is the time-out probability. As \(T\to\infty\) this collapses to the scale-function result of Section 3.3, and \(P_{\text{pass}}+P_{\text{bust}}\to 1\). Both checks pass numerically. (Implementation: 400–600 terms; a Monte-Carlo fallback covers the small-\(\sigma\)/large-\(|\mu|\) corner. See code/barrier_core.py.)

Case\(\mu\) ($/day)\(\sigma\) ($/day)\(P_{\text{pass}}\) (analytic)\(P_{\text{pass}}\) (MC)\(P_{\text{bust}}\) (MC)
Zero edge07000.11680.10920.4191
Positive edge+607000.22630.21350.2733
Negative edge−607000.05210.04810.5826

The analytic (continuous-monitoring) value sits just above the discrete Monte-Carlo, as theory predicts. Note the headline already: a zero-edge trader risking $700/day passes only ≈ 11–12% of the time in 30 days — about a third of the already-modest 1/3 perpetual ceiling, the rest eaten by Theta.

4. The Greeks of an Evaluation

We treat the pass probability \(P_{\text{pass}}\) as the object of interest (the risk-neutral price of the digital is $e^{-rT}\Pi\,P_{\text{pass}}^{\mathbb Q}$, so probability Greeks and price Greeks differ only by constants). With current P&L \(X\) and time-to-maturity \(\tau = T-t\):

\[ \Theta = \frac{\partial P_{\text{pass}}}{\partial t} = -\frac{\partial P_{\text{pass}}}{\partial \tau},\quad \nu_{\text{Vega}} = \frac{\partial P_{\text{pass}}}{\partial \sigma},\quad \Delta = \frac{\partial P_{\text{pass}}}{\partial X},\quad \Gamma = \frac{\partial^2 P_{\text{pass}}}{\partial X^2}, \]

computed by central differences on the closed form.

4.1 Theta (\(\Theta\)): the clock is the firm's ally

Because the upper barrier is a knock-in, time spent not-yet-touching +$6,000 is time that cannot be recovered, and the distance to travel (\(b = 6000\)) is large.

Figure 2. Left: pass probability versus time remaining for an edgeless trader at break-even P&L, at three risk levels. Right: the Theta felt day-by-day by a trader whose P&L is treading water.

Risk\(P_{\text{pass}}\) with 30 days left\(P_{\text{pass}}\) with 2 days left
\(\sigma = \$800\)/day0.164≈ 0.000
\(\sigma = \$500\)/day0.028≈ 0.000

By the final two days, a trader who has not already banked most of the +$6,000 has a pass probability indistinguishable from zero: there is no longer enough time for diffusion to span the gap to the target. Theta quietly converts the majority of accounts — neither far ahead nor yet busted — to worthless.

4.2 Vega (\(\nu_{\text{Vega}}\)): a lever that is capped

Because Theta is lethal, the edgeless trader's only way to reach the target in time is to widen the distribution — raise \(\sigma\). But here the arithmetic geometry bites in a way the equity model did not.

Figure 3. Pass probability versus daily dollar-volatility. For zero/negative edge it rises monotonically with \(\sigma\) but is asymptotically capped at 1/3 (dashed). For positive edge it has an interior optimum (here $\sigma^\star \approx $1{,}410\(, \)P\approx 0.38$). Shaded: the volatility the rules actually permit.

Three facts:

  1. Edgeless Vega is positive but bounded. For \(\mu \le 0\), \(P_{\text{pass}}\)

is increasing in \(\sigma\) — the trader is mathematically incentivised to take more risk — yet no amount of volatility can beat the 1/3 ceiling, and inside the permitted band the pass probability is only \~0.05–0.17. The edgeless trader is structurally trapped below one in three.

  1. Skill creates a finite optimum. For a positive-edge trader the curve

humps and then declines toward 1/3: too much \(\sigma\) washes out the drift advantage. The optimum is a modest risk level that sits near or inside the permitted band. As in the equity analysis, the sign and shape of Vega is a litmus test for edge — and the rules, by capping \(\sigma\), implicitly test exactly that.

  1. The rules confiscate the only lever the edgeless trader has. Capping

\(\sigma\) barely matters to the skilled trader (whose optimum is already low) and is devastating to the edgeless one (Section 7.3).

4.3 Delta (\(\Delta\)) and Gamma (\(\Gamma\)): forced position sizing

Figure 4. Delta (left) and Gamma (right) of the pass probability versus current cumulative P&L, at three points in the cycle. Dashed lines mark the barriers and break-even.

  • Delta — marginal pass-probability per dollar of P&L — is largest in the

interior and near the target late in the cycle, when little time remains and each dollar moves you across the now-narrow remaining gap.

  • Gamma is the destabiliser. Approaching the target with little time left,

Gamma is large and positive: small favourable moves sharply raise the pass probability, rationally inviting the trader to press size to lock the touch. Approaching the trailing floor, the convexity and the daily limit conspire to knock the account out before any "martingale out of the hole" can pay. In options language the trader is short Gamma against the clock — the position demands its largest adjustments exactly when it is most fragile, which is what the daily-loss and trailing rules exist to exploit.

5. From Trading Style to \((\mu, \sigma)\)

We parametrise \((\mu,\sigma)\) by win rate \(p\), reward-to-risk \(R\), and dollar risk per trade \(k\) (the stop, in dollars), under fixed-size futures trading. Each trade adds \(+Rk\) with probability \(p\) or \(-k\) with probability \(1-p\). With \(n\) trades/day (\(n=4\)):

\[ \mu = n\big[k(p(1+R)-1) - \text{cost}\big],\qquad \sigma = k\sqrt{n\big[\,pR^2 + (1-p) - (p(1+R)-1)^2\,\big]} . \]

Two structural facts:

  • Dollar risk \(k\) controls \(\sigma\) linearly. The max-contract limit, the

daily loss limit, and the consistency rule are all, ultimately, caps on \(k\) and hence on \(\sigma\).

  • Skill \((p,R)\) controls \(\mu\), with the zero-edge frontier at

\(p = 1/(1+R)\). Unlike the equity model there is no volatility drag, so a break-even trader sits exactly at \(\mu = 0\) — but trading costs (commissions, exchange fees, slippage) push real traders to \(\mu < 0\).

5.1 Skew profiles (on the zero-edge frontier)

  • Scalper / negative skew (\(p=0.667\), \(R=0.5\)): many small wins, rare large

losses; low \(\sigma \approx \$495\)/day. This is the "responsible," consistent style the rules nominally reward.

  • Symmetric (\(p=0.5\), \(R=1\)): \(\sigma \approx \$700\)/day.
  • Trend / positive skew (\(p=0.333\), \(R=2\)): many small losses, rare large

wins; high \(\sigma \approx \$990\)/day.

Because Vega is positive, the model predicts the high-\(\sigma\) positive-skew style passes most often — the Monte-Carlo confirms it (Section 6.2), with the uncomfortable corollary that the prudent low-\(\sigma\) scalper is the least likely to pass.

6. Monte-Carlo Study

6.1 Engine and assumptions

A vectorised trade-level Monte-Carlo (simulate_challenge_mc) simulates P&L trade-by-trade (4 trades/day × 30 days), monitors both barriers discretely, applies the trailing high-water-mark drawdown (locking at break-even), the $2,000 daily loss limit, and the 50% consistency rule (a pass requires the best single day to be ≤ 50% of total profit), with optional adverse jumps. Up to 100,000 paths per configuration, fixed seeds.

Figure 5. Sixty P&L paths for a zero-edge trader risking $350/trade. Green = passed (+$6,000), red = busted (trailing −$3,000), grey = timed out. The target sits twice as far from the start as the floor.

6.2 The probability matrix and the skew result

Figure 6. Monte-Carlo pass probability over \((R, p)\) at $350 risk/trade under the full rule set. Dashed white: the zero-edge frontier \(p=1/(1+R)\); contours at 0.10, 0.20, 0.35.

Pass probability is organised by which side of the zero-edge frontier the trader is on — i.e. by genuine edge — but even well above the frontier it is held down by the 2:1 geometry and the rules. Holding edge at zero and varying skew:

Profile\((p,R)\)\(\sigma\) ($/day)PassBustTime-out
Scalper (neg. skew)\((0.667,\,0.5)\)4950.0190.4380.543
Symmetric\((0.5,\,1.0)\)7000.0910.6790.229
Trend (pos. skew)\((0.333,\,2.0)\)9900.1650.7860.049

The "responsible," consistent scalper — exactly the trader the rules claim to cultivate — passes 1.9% of the time. The high-variance trend trader passes most (16.5%) but busts 79% of the time. Variance is the only route to the target, and the rules forbid variance.

6.3 The rule set is a volatility cap

Adding the rules one at a time to the risk sweep:

Figure 7. Pass probability versus \(\sigma\) under four rule regimes. Each added rule peels back the high-\(\sigma\) region where the pass probability would otherwise climb toward the 1/3 ceiling.

Rule regimePeak \(P_{\text{pass}}\)
Static max-loss only0.314
+ trailing drawdown0.221
+ $2,000 daily limit0.173
+ 50% consistency0.170

The static contract lets a high-\(\sigma\) gambler approach the 1/3 ceiling (0.31); the trailing drawdown, daily limit, and consistency rule together cut the attainable peak roughly in half (to 0.17) and make the high-\(\sigma\) region unsurvivable. The rules do not change what the trader should do to pass (take variance); they change whether it works (it no longer does).

6.4 Jump-diffusion robustness

Figure 8. Adding Merton-style adverse gaps lowers the ceiling further; the qualitative picture is unchanged.

Pure diffusion0.175
Jumps: 2% prob, −$3k gap0.103

Adverse gaps make the trailing floor and daily limit easier to hit, so they only worsen the buyer's odds. The double-barrier structure and the \(\sigma\)-cap mechanism are robust to the diffusion assumption.

7. The Economics: Is It a Fair Bet?

7.1 The prize is a capped second barrier option

Passing delivers not cash but a funded account, which is itself a trailing double-barrier game: keep P&L above a trailing −$3,000 floor while skimming profits, of which the trader keeps a high split \(s\approx 90\%\) — but subject to payout caps (the card's "DOUBLE Payout Caps") and minimum-period rules. We model the funded phase honestly (simulate_funded_extraction): trailing floor locking at break-even, profit skimmed every 10 days up to a per-period cap, terminal death on the floor. The expected cash extracted, \(\Pi(\mu,\sigma)\), is the true prize — and it is bounded, because the caps truncate exactly the high-variance upside a lucky funded trader would otherwise realise.

7.2 Net expected value and the break-even edge

With recurring fee \(F = \$129\),

\[ \mathrm{EV} = P_{\text{pass}}(\mu,\sigma,T)\cdot\Pi(\mu,\sigma) - F . \]

Figure 9. Left: net expected value of the evaluation versus the trader's genuine win rate (1:1 reward-to-risk, $350 risk/trade). Right: the two components — challenge pass probability and capped funded extraction.

The break-even win rate is ≈ 50.1% — i.e. you need a genuinely positive edge (above a coin flip) merely to break even, before counting trading costs. At an honest coin flip (\(p = 0.5\)) the pass probability is 8.7% and the journey is negative-EV (≈ −$21 per cycle on our generous, high-split, no-cost funded model). This is the decisive contrast with the trader-favourable +8%/−10% equity contract: the 2:1 futures geometry makes the evaluation a negative-expected-value purchase for every trader without a real, positive edge — and once commissions, exchange fees, and slippage push \(\mu\) below zero, the negativity deepens and the break-even edge rises further.

7.3 The real mechanism: the volatility filter

The \(\sigma\)-cap imposed by the trailing/daily/consistency rules has a wildly asymmetric effect by edge. Comparing each trader's best attainable pass probability (taking as much variance as they like) against the pass probability the rules permit (\(\sigma \approx \$600\)/day):

Figure 10. Best-attainable versus rule-permitted pass probability, by edge. The relative haircut shrinks monotonically as edge grows.

TraderBest attainable \(P_{\text{pass}}\)Under the rules (\(\sigma{=}\$600\))Haircut
Negative edge (−$60/day)0.3120.022−93%
Zero edge0.3330.067−80%
Mild positive edge (+$60/day)0.3780.164−57%
Strong positive edge (+$150/day)0.5040.423−16%

This is the thesis quantified. The volatility cap is the product. It is not risk management for the trader; it is an edge filter whose relative bite falls monotonically with edge — from −93% for the negative-edge trader to just −16% for a strongly skilled one, who barely needs variance because drift carries them. The rule set removes the variance pathway to the target, which is the only pathway available to the edgeless majority. With variance gone, Theta (Section 4.1) drives their pass probability toward zero as the month ends.

7.4 Where the house edge comes from

The futures evaluation's economics rest on three stacked layers, none of which is a hidden fee markup:

  1. Geometry. 2:1 caps the edgeless ceiling at 1/3 before anything else

happens (Section 3.3).

  1. Theta. The 30-day clock cuts the realistic pass probability to \~1 in 10

(Sections 3.5, 4.1).

  1. The \(\sigma\)-cap. The "Responsible Trading" rules remove the variance

pathway, filtering out precisely the edgeless majority (Section 7.3), while a capped, split-reduced funded payoff bounds the firm's liability on the rare winner (Section 7.1).

The marketing sells the target ("hit +$6,000"); the rules enforce the unstated requirement ("possess a genuine edge, and never use the variance that could substitute for one"); the recurring fee is collected from everyone in between. A secondary, well-documented channel — internalising (B-booking) simulated order flow — means failed and timed-out accounts are pure fee revenue, but our model needs no such assumption: the geometry, Theta, and the \(\sigma\)-filter already explain the edge.

8. Discussion and Limitations

  • Fixed-size discipline flatters the trader. Our trader never over-sizes

beyond a constant \(k\), never revenge-trades, and has stationary \((p,R)\). Real evaluation buyers do all three, inflating realised \(\sigma\) into the bust region and depressing \(\mu\) — pushing outcomes further in the firm's favour than shown. Our pass probabilities are upper bounds for the typical buyer.

  • Costs are excluded from the headline. We set per-trade cost to zero in the

EV; real futures fees/slippage make \(\mu < 0\) and raise the break-even edge.

  • Arithmetic BM is an idealisation. Streaks, fat tails, and intraday

seasonality matter; the jump-diffusion check (Section 6.4) addresses tails and only strengthens the conclusion.

  • The funded value \(\Pi\) is model-dependent and was chosen generously to the

trader (90% split, modest caps). Tighter caps, minimum-day rules, or discretionary payout frictions lower \(\Pi\) and push break-even higher.

  • General, not firm-specific. The supplied card is a concrete instance; the

framework is parametric. Substitute any firm's \(U\), \(|D|\), daily limit, consistency, \(T\), split, and caps in code/.

None of these caveats touches the structural identity (Section 2), the 2:1 geometry ceiling (Section 3.3), or the volatility-filter result (Section 7.3) — the load-bearing claims.

9. Conclusion

A futures proprietary-trading evaluation is, exactly, a discrete double-barrier one-touch binary option on cumulative P&L: the target is an upper knock-in digital, the max-loss "One Rule" is a trailing lower knock-out, and the monthly cycle is maturity. We priced it in closed form, validated by Monte-Carlo, and computed its Greeks.

The design is laid bare by three numbers. Geometry: the 2:1 reward-to-risk caps an edgeless trader's lifetime pass probability at 1/3. Theta: the 30-day clock cuts the realistic figure to \~1 in 10, and to essentially zero in the final days. The \(\sigma\)-cap: the trailing drawdown, $2,000 daily limit, and 50% consistency rule — the "Responsible Trading Advantage" — strip 80–93% of the pass probability from zero/negative-edge traders while costing a skilled trader little, because variance is the edgeless trader's only path to a target set twice as far as ruin.

Unlike a trader-favourable equity-percentage contract, the futures 2:1 structure is negative expected value for anyone without a genuine, positive edge — the break-even win rate is at the coin flip before costs and above it after. The prudent, low-volatility "consistent" trader the rules claim to reward is, in our simulation, the least likely to pass (1.9%).

The consistency rule and daily drawdown limit are not there to protect the trader's capital. They are there to cap the trader's \(\sigma\), so that — against a target set twice as far as the bust level — Theta kills the option before it can ever touch the upper barrier. That is the predation: not in the premium, but in the geometry and the Greeks.

Appendix A. Derivation of the finite-horizon pass probability

Solve \(\partial_t p = -\mu\,\partial_y p + \tfrac12\sigma^2\partial_{yy}p\) on \((0,L)\) with \(p(0,t)=p(L,t)=0\), \(p(y,0)=\delta(y-y_0)\). The \(h\)-transform \(p = e^{\frac{\mu}{\sigma^2}(y-y_0)-\frac{\mu^2}{2\sigma^2}t}q\) reduces this to the heat equation \(\partial_t q = \tfrac12\sigma^2\partial_{yy}q\) with the same Dirichlet data, whose eigenexpansion is $q=\tfrac2L\sum_n \sin\frac{n\pi y_0}{L}\sin\frac{n\pi y}{L}e^{-\frac12\sigma^2\lambda_n t}\(, \)\lambda_n = (n\pi/L)^2\(. The upper-boundary flux \)J_U = -\tfrac12\sigma^2\partial_y p|_{y=L}\( (using \)\partial_y\sin\frac{n\pi y}{L}|_L = \frac{n\pi}{L}(-1)^n$) and \(\int_0^T e^{-\beta_n t}dt = (1-e^{-\beta_n T})/\beta_n\) give the boxed formula of Section 3.4. The lower-boundary flux gives \(P_{\text{bust}}\). \(\square\)

Appendix B. Numerical methods and reproducibility

  • Closed form: series truncated at \(N=400\)–\(600\); convergence verified by the

\(T\to\infty\) identity \(P_{\text{pass}}+P_{\text{bust}}\to 1\) and the scale-function limit \(\to 1/3\).

  • Greeks: central finite differences on the closed form.
  • Monte-Carlo: vectorised NumPy, fixed seeds, up to 100k paths/config,

discrete (per-trade) barrier monitoring; trailing DD, daily limit, and consistency enforced as in the contract.

  • Stability: prob_pass_safe falls back to arithmetic-BM Monte-Carlo in the

rare unstable corner.
